stories.headline: House Ethics Committee Finds 'Substantial Evidence' Rep. Jimmy Gomez Made Unwanted Sexual Advances
stories.summary:
The House Ethics Committee announced Monday that it found "substantial evidence" that Rep. Jimmy Gomez, a California Democrat, made unwanted sexual advances toward a House staffer, conduct the panel said could constitute sexual assault.

The committee's findings drew on interviews with a woman who said Gomez made unwanted advances toward her on two occasions while she worked as a House staffer. One encounter, at a bar, involved what the committee described as "sexual contact." In the other, in his congressional office, he was described as "forceful."

The report was covered by outlets across the political spectrum, including wire, left-leaning and right-leaning publications. Further steps could include recommendations for discipline, though the available reporting did not specify what action the committee or the full House might take. The findings arrive as Democrats prepare to take control of the House with their largest majority since 1992, which may raise the political stakes of any response.

stories.headline: Trump Directs Justice Department to Seek Death Penalty in Child Murder Cases, Criticizes Newsom Clemency Plan
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump announced Monday that he is directing the Justice Department to seek the death penalty in federal child murder cases and in cases in which rapists or human traffickers kill their victims. He made the announcement in a speech at DOJ headquarters before an audience that included victims' families.

Trump also condemned outgoing California Gov. Gavin Newsom's plan to commute 548 state death sentences to life without parole. The federal directive would have no legal effect on Newsom's plan, since those sentences were imposed under state law.

Supporters of expanded capital punishment argue that the most heinous crimes against children and trafficking victims warrant the ultimate penalty and that it serves justice for victims' families. Opponents of the death penalty, including Newsom and many Democrats, have argued it is applied unevenly, risks executing innocent people and is not proven to deter crime. Newsom's clemency plan has drawn criticism from prosecutors and victims' advocates who oppose the commutations.

The directive is expected to guide federal prosecutors' charging decisions going forward.

stories.headline: Update: Mexican Soldiers Attacked as Eight Alleged Cartel Members Detained After 'Chapo Isidro' Arrest
stories.summary:
Mexican soldiers detained eight alleged members of a cartel after being shot at on Sunday while on patrol in Sinaloa de Leyva, in northern Sinaloa state. The defense ministry said the soldiers were trying to restore order after Friday's arrest of cartel leader Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "Chapo Isidro."

The ministry said the eight detainees, one of them a minor, were also involved in retaliatory violence after the arrest. Special forces seized six vehicles, two of them armored and fitted with gun turrets. The defense minister said Monday that four soldiers and 16 members of organized crime were killed in the raid and firefight, according to the latest figures.

Meza Flores, 44, was on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted list. His second-in-command, known as "Serafin," and his financial operator were also arrested and flown to Mexico City. The U.S. Justice Department called the operation "spectacular" and praised the bilateral effort, with Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva calling him "the most dangerous man in Mexico." After the arrest, cartel members blocked roads and burned vehicles and shops.

stories.headline: More Than 12,000 Evacuated From Manchester Concert After Unknown Irritant Sickens Fans
stories.summary:
More than 12,000 fans were evacuated from a Don Toliver concert at Co-op Live arena in Manchester, England, after an unknown irritant was released in the crowd, authorities said Monday. Greater Manchester Police were called around 10 p.m. Sunday and declared a "major incident," allowing emergency services to coordinate.

The North West Ambulance Service said one person was taken to hospital and more than 80 were assessed at the scene, some with eye and respiratory symptoms. The substance was initially believed to be tear gas. Decontamination was carried out as a precaution. Concertgoers described coughing, itchy eyes and a "horrible smell," and said it was nearly an hour before an announcement ended the show.

Police Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker urged anyone who later became unwell to go to a local hospital and said investigators would work to determine what the substance was. Prime Minister Andy Burnham's spokesman called the incident "deeply worrying." The venue is about two miles from Manchester Arena, where 22 people were killed in a 2017 bombing. Toliver is scheduled to perform in London on Monday and Tuesday.

stories.headline: Trump-Era Grant Cuts Halt Medical Studies in Black Communities, Researchers Sue NIH
stories.summary:
A study in Pittsburgh aimed at understanding why Black Americans are about twice as likely to develop Alzheimer's disease has been abruptly halted, one of a growing number of research projects affected as the administration searches for and ends medical grants whose descriptions include words such as "disparities," "minority" and "racial." Lead researcher Andrea Rosso is among numerous scientists named in a recently filed lawsuit against the National Institutes of Health and its parent Department of Health and Human Services.

The suit is one of a growing body of legal actions challenging the terminations. Researchers argue that the cuts disrupt long-running studies, waste money already spent, and leave gaps in knowledge about diseases that affect some populations more severely than others.

The administration has framed its review of grants as an effort to end spending on diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives it considers ideological and to redirect federal research dollars toward priorities it says benefit all Americans. Supporters of that approach argue that research should be judged on scientific merit rather than demographic categories. Critics, including many scientists and Democratic lawmakers, counter that studying health disparities is core medical science and that halting such work undermines treatment for millions of people.

The lawsuits are expected to continue moving through the courts, and the outcome could determine whether studies like Rosso's can resume or whether other terminated projects are restored. Democrats, who will control the House starting in January, have signaled they intend to use oversight powers to scrutinize the administration's health and research policies.

stories.headline: Update: Huang's Nvidia Return Draws Bipartisan Criticism in Congress; Senate Sets Dec. 3 Testimony
stories.summary:
Lawmakers from both parties criticized Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, less than two weeks after he resigned amid a scandal over an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China. Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) asked on social media, "No national security risk? Based on what," and Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) said Huang's behavior does not support his return.

The new development is the congressional response and a firm testimony date. A powerful Senate committee chairman said Huang will testify publicly on Dec. 3, and congressional panels confirmed he is still expected to answer questions. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is pushing to attach tighter AI export controls to the 2027 National Defense Authorization Act. Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on House Oversight, and Sen. Chris Van Hollen also voiced concern, and Sen. Ruben Gallego called Trump's role "as close to socialism, communism as I've ever seen."

President Trump, who said he spoke "directly and indirectly" with the board and "convinced them," says the government has no reason to believe Huang's return is a national security risk. Axios reported that allies argued Huang was "too big to fail" for the economy and a victim of "deep state" maneuvering. Supporters see the move as protecting a company central to U.S. AI leadership and market stability, while critics say a president put the weight of his office behind a private personnel decision despite intelligence concerns.

Democrats, who take control of the House in January, are eager to deploy investigative powers, creating a headache for Republicans who must now weigh the White House position against national security worries.

stories.headline: Iran Flogs Singer Parastoo Ahmadi and Band Members for Performing Without Hijab
stories.summary:
Iranian authorities have flogged prominent singer Parastoo Ahmadi, 29, and four members of her band and production team, lawyers told the BBC. Ahmadi and four male co-defendants each received 74 lashes at a sentence enforcement office in the city of Qom, a defense lawyer said on Monday.

Ahmadi wore a sleeveless dress during a concert livestreamed in December 2024. Iranian law bans public performances by women and requires women above the age of puberty to cover their hair and wear loose clothing. In June a Qom criminal court convicted her and eight others of "offending public decency" by publishing "obscene and indecent material," which they denied. They were also banned from audiovisual work and from leaving the country for two years. An appeals court upheld the sentence at the end of September.

Lawyers said they tried to overturn or reduce the verdict and to postpone enforcement, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately. The Center for Human Rights in Iran called the flogging "a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights" and a demonstration of the authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms. Rights groups say flogging constitutes cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment under the international prohibition on torture.

The case echoes the backlash after the 2022 death in custody of Mahsa Amini, which set off nationwide protests in which hundreds were killed in a crackdown. Many Iranian artists condemned Ahmadi's sentence when it was issued.

stories.headline: India Pledges $1.6 Billion to Nepal in Reset of Ties During Prime Minister Shah's Delhi Visit
stories.summary:
India has pledged nearly $1.6 billion in support to Nepal during Prime Minister Balen Shah's first visit to Delhi, as the two neighbors sought to reset a relationship strained by years of friction. Most of the package will come as a line of credit for energy projects, with about $400 million in grants for reconstruction and infrastructure.

The countries also announced agreements on trade, hydropower, transport and education for Nepali youths, and Shah and Prime Minister Narendra Modi jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service. Shah, 36, a former rapper, rose to power after Gen Z-led protests toppled his predecessor.

The aid comes as Nepal recovers from devastating floods earlier this year that killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing. The government estimates rebuilding could cost as much as $4.8 billion, and Shah has faced criticism over support for affected families. Nepal would have preferred a larger package, but former diplomat Vijay Kant Karna called it "a significant amount" that could help stabilize ties.

Nepal is wedged between India and China, and allegations of political interference and an unresolved border dispute have often complicated relations with Delhi. The border dispute was largely absent from public remarks, though the joint statement acknowledged outstanding issues remained. Analysts suggested Shah chose to set contentious matters aside to secure progress on immediate development needs.

stories.headline: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO, Shares Surge and Markets Rebound; Schumer Vows Investigation
stories.summary:
Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, and the company's shares jumped roughly 27 to 33 percent at the open. The stock opened near $167, about $35.50 above Friday's close. The move followed reports that Huang had been targeted in an alleged foreign intelligence operation. U.S. intelligence is said to show that a woman at the center of an AI chip scandal, who had been in a relationship with Huang, was in contact with China's Ministry of State Security.

Broader markets rebounded sharply after a bruising sell-off. The Nasdaq rose about 6 percent after the opening bell, erasing Friday's losses, when it suffered its second-worst day of 2026. The S&P 500 and Dow had fallen into correction territory, and the S&P 500 recovered nearly half of last week's losses, among its worst weeks since the 2008 financial crisis.

President Trump said he spoke directly and indirectly with Nvidia's board, called the decision "correct and proper," and said Huang's return poses no national security risk. He also posted a doctored image of Huang in the pose from his 2024 Pennsylvania rally. Supporters of the administration framed the episode as evidence of aggressive Chinese espionage.

Democrats criticized the reinstatement. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Democrats will use their "full power" to investigate Huang and other executives, saying the administration's rush to reinstate him underscores the need for congressional action. Sen. John Kennedy has separately asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to testify under oath over claims that China circumvented chip export controls.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Says Drones Sank Russian Corvette in Libya as Russian 'Triple-Tap' Strike Hits Zelensky's Home City
stories.summary:
Russia's war in Ukraine continued to escalate on Monday. A Russian "triple-tap" attack in Zelensky's home city killed an emergency worker and a 7-year-old child. Airstrikes on an apartment block in Dymer, near Kyiv, killed at least 11 people on Sunday, and Zelensky vowed that "absolutely deserved retaliations will come." A foreign national injured in Kyiv has been identified as a U.S. citizen.

New details emerged on Ukraine's strike on a Russian vessel in Libya. Zelensky released video showing the corvette Merkury, one of Russia's newest ships, attacked at the Benghazi naval base, and said seven drones were used in an operation involving special forces. A Russian cargo ship was also hit. The Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region" but declined to comment directly.

Security concerns are spreading beyond Ukraine. Prosecutors say three Russian missiles flew into Poland on Friday, and NATO will deploy an airborne warning and control aircraft to monitor the country's eastern region. Western intelligence agencies have also warned that Russia has built a satellite designed to carry a nuclear warhead that could launch as soon as next month. Denmark is expected to ask the EU for tougher measures against Russia, and Poland said it would support them.

In Washington, President Trump defended his relationship with Putin. California Gov. Gavin Newsom visited Ukraine and announced a donation of medical supplies.

stories.headline: Update: COP31 Climate Talks Collapse in Antalya Over Fossil Fuel Language
stories.summary:
The COP31 climate conference ended on Sunday in Antalya, Turkey, without an agreement after delegates failed to resolve a dispute over fossil fuel wording. The proposed Antalya Pact made no mention of fossil fuels, while the COP28 deal in Dubai three years ago had committed to transitioning away from them. Several countries said they could not accept a text that omitted the language, fearing it would weaken the Dubai commitment.

Some opposition was voiced publicly. A Saudi negotiator, speaking for the 22 Arab League states, said Arab nations contributed less than 2 percent of historical emissions and have the right to choose their own approaches. Russia's delegate said cutting oil and gas supply before demand falls would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty, and that Russia could not accept any fossil fuel formulation.

Australia's Chris Bowen, who led the negotiations, cited the "most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory" and "unbridgeable red lines." Turkey's environment minister Murat Kurum, the summit president, argued governments should not get "hung up on one word or phrase."

The United States sent no official delegation, as President Trump has rejected the international climate process. While talks failed, Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen pledging to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products. Observers say attention may now shift to smaller agreements, local leaders and the growth of clean energy.

stories.headline: Virginia and Oregon Sue SpaceX Over Grok AI Deepfake Porn and Child Sexual Abuse Material
stories.summary:
Virginia and Oregon announced separate lawsuits on Monday against SpaceX, which owns the xAI tool Grok. They are the first state attorneys general to sue over the issue. The complaints, filed by Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, both Democrats, allege that the company created and promoted AI deepfake pornography and sexually explicit images of children.

Virginia's suit accuses the company of failing to prevent Grok from generating sexualized images of people, including children, without their knowledge or consent. The states say the company's Grok Imagine tool violated consumer protection laws, and the complaints reference the company's marketing of the feature.

The cases add legal pressure on Elon Musk's AI business at a time when SpaceX is also renting computing power from its data centers to competitors, including Anthropic, which reportedly makes it harder for its own AI effort. Musk is an investor in Skydance, the parent company of CBS News, which covered the suits.

The lawsuits are likely to test how state consumer protection law applies to AI-generated content. Responses from SpaceX and further actions by other states were not detailed in initial reports.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Says He Is Inclined to Strike Iran After New Year If No Deal Is Reached
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump said he is inclined to resume strikes against Iran after the New Year if Washington and Tehran do not reach a deal to end the conflict. He acknowledged that indirect talks between the two countries are still under way, but described Iranian negotiators as "professional tap dancers" and accused the government in Tehran of stalling. He also dismissed the talks as meaningless while the U.S. naval blockade remains in place.

The remarks add a more distant timeline to a story that has been moving quickly. Earlier today, the digest reported that the U.S. had delayed a possible strike on Iran as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed for a joint offensive. Trump also told an Israeli outlet that he may not decide on his next move in the Iran war until 2027.

Netanyahu has called renewing strikes a matter of national security. Military analysts and opposition leaders in Israel say he is prioritizing his own political interests. Supporters of the president's approach say continued military and economic pressure is needed to force concessions from Tehran. Critics say open-ended threats and the blockade risk deeper regional escalation and give Iran little incentive to negotiate.

The next steps depend on whether the indirect talks produce any movement before the new year. The blockade remains in force in the meantime.

stories.headline: Oxfam Report Says Gaza Contaminated, Calls Israeli Attacks 'Environmental War Crimes'
stories.summary:
A new report from Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory says more than 99 percent of Gaza shows indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks. The groups used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and open-source data. They describe it as the most comprehensive assessment to date of the environmental damage from three years of war.

The report cites heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and dioxins and biological contaminants in the air, soil and water. Oxfam International executive director Amitabh Behar accused Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza." Report author Lama Abdul Samad said long-term health effects could include respiratory disease, cancers, organ damage, birth defects and stillbirths. All six wastewater treatment plants are out of operation, and sewage is reaching groundwater and the Mediterranean. Winter storms have worsened conditions in tent sites housing displaced people.

The report draws on earlier figures. A United Nations Environment Programme estimate last year put debris from destroyed buildings at more than 61 million tonnes, with about 15 percent potentially carrying a high risk of hazardous contamination. A UN special rapporteur said in February that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives had been dropped on Gaza.

Israel has been asked for a response. It rejects genocide accusations in the ongoing International Court of Justice case as baseless and distorted. It says its campaign is self-defense against Hamas after the October 7, 2023 attack and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm. Laboratory destruction and Israeli restrictions on equipment entering Gaza limit on-the-ground testing.

stories.headline: Update: Clayton to Serve as Acting National Cyber Director as Davies Awaits Confirmation
stories.summary:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will also serve as acting national cyber director while Kirsten Davies awaits Senate confirmation to lead the office, Axios reported. A White House official said the strong support Davies received convinced President Trump to nominate her permanently rather than keep her in an acting capacity.

The move places the nation's top intelligence official in charge of coordinating cybersecurity policy. It comes amid recent technology outages and reported cyberattacks, including a confirmed hack targeting the FBI's National Crime Information Center database. The previous national cyber director was fired last week, and Trump said a week of tech outages was unrelated.

The confirmation faces some resistance. Sen. Thom Tillis previously blocked a vote on Trump's cybersecurity agency nominee over remarks about January 6. Supporters of the arrangement say it provides continuity and senior leadership during a period of heightened threats. Critics, including Democrats who have questioned the firing, may see combining the roles as concentrating authority during a vulnerable moment.

The arrangement lasts until the Senate acts on Davies's nomination. Democrats take control of the House in January, which could affect oversight of the office.

stories.headline: Belgium Strike Halts Flights and Transit Over Austerity Plans
stories.summary:
A nationwide strike against planned austerity measures has cancelled hundreds of flights and severely disrupted public transport across Belgium. Air traffic controllers halted all traffic at Brussels Airport and Charleroi between 07:00 and 21:00 local time. A Brussels Airport spokesperson said 404 flights could not operate, affecting more than 50,000 passengers. Underground services in Brussels were also halted.

Tens of thousands joined a protest march in the capital. Teachers and other public-sector workers said education and services are being starved of funding. The strike comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with coalition partners on a budget meant to cut borrowing costs. King Philippe declined De Wever's resignation earlier this month to allow more time for negotiation.

The five-party coalition is split. The socialist Vooruit refuses to endorse plans agreed by the other four and wants higher taxes on the wealthy and smaller cuts to pensions and health spending. Union leaders, including FGTB head Bert Engelaar, called for a genuine wealth tax and an end to tax loopholes. CSC leader Ann Vermorgen criticized plans to cut bank holidays that fall on weekends.

De Wever met the king for the third update on the impasse. The palace said the king regretted the lack of significant progress and urged an agreement as soon as possible.

stories.headline: Update: US Delays Possible Iran Strike as Netanyahu Presses for Joint Offensive
stories.summary:
The United States has decided to postpone any potential military strike on Iran by at least a week, despite pressure from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for a joint offensive, Israeli outlet Ynet reported Sunday, citing US administration officials. CBS News, citing sources familiar with the matter, reported that Israel and the US are weighing a new assault in the short term. Israeli officials are said to be concerned about how quickly Iran is rebuilding its ballistic missile manufacturing and moving military and nuclear infrastructure underground.

Israeli Military Intelligence reportedly assesses that a strike could ignite "multiple fronts," contradicting alleged expectations by Netanyahu and Mossad chief Roman Gofman that an operation could stay limited to three to five days. Opposition politician Avigdor Liberman has warned against an attack, reportedly out of concern that Netanyahu could consider a unilateral strike without American approval. Critics cited by The New York Times argue that Netanyahu's push cannot be separated from his efforts to retain power, while supporters point to the pace of Iran's rebuilding as a genuine security threat.

President Trump told Fox News he might resume the war on Iran next year if talks fail to produce a diplomatic resolution, blaming his party's midterm losses for what he called Tehran's increasingly aggressive policies. He has also dismissed Iranian negotiators as "professional tap dancers" while a US naval blockade holds. Iran has vowed to force the US to lift the blockade and continues to attack Bahrain, while Houthi militants have targeted Saudi Arabia, though the oil supply outlook remains robust.

stories.headline: Ukraine Claims Sinking of Russian Warship Merkury at Libyan Port
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed Monday that Kyiv was responsible for sinking the Russian navy corvette Merkury, docked at the Libyan port of Benghazi. Libyan officials said the vessel was struck by two sea drones Sunday, causing an explosion and fire. Zelenskyy described the operation as "exemplary" and said a sanctioned dry cargo vessel was also damaged.

The Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region" but declined to comment directly on the attacks. The strike followed a separate drone attack on a Russia-bound cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday, which Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind; Kyiv has not commented on that incident. Analysts say the series of strikes on Russian vessels far from Ukraine fuels fears that the war could spread.

The attacks come days after Vladimir Putin promised a "painful" response to Ukrainian strikes, and Russia has since launched further missile and drone attacks, including on Dymer in the Kyiv region, where eleven people have been confirmed dead. Zelenskyy has also criticized President Trump's description of Putin as a "friend" after their trilateral meeting with China's Xi Jinping. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Sunday he trusts Trump completely and drew a distinction between personal rapport and national interests, while Democrats called the remarks a betrayal of American values.

stories.headline: DNC Announces 12 Primary Debates for 2028, Limits Candidates' Ties to Dark-Money Groups
stories.summary:
The Democratic National Committee announced Monday that it will hold 12 presidential primary debates for the 2028 cycle, with the first in June 2027 and five scheduled for next year. Chair Ken Martin is also moving to restrict candidates' ties to super PACs and dark-money groups, requiring participants to pledge to denounce spending from supportive groups that do not disclose their donors.

Axios reported the rules could complicate the plans of likely candidates, many of whom were expected to rely on super PACs to boost their messaging and attack rivals. The shift sets up a potential clash between the party chair and campaigns that are soon to launch. Debate participation is conditioned on the pledge.

The announcement comes as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress in January after sweeping midterm wins, including their largest House majority since 1992. Supporters of the rules frame them as a push for transparency and reduced outside money, while critics argue they could handicap Democrats against Republican-aligned groups that face no such limits. Potential candidates, including figures such as Rahm Emanuel, are already discussing what direction the party should take.

stories.headline: Update: US Stock Futures Rebound After Friday's AI-Driven Selloff
stories.summary:
US equity-index futures rallied Monday as buyers returned following Friday's selloff in artificial intelligence companies. Treasury futures fell as demand for haven assets ebbed. Early moves pointed to some stability when regular trading resumes, though analysts warned of more volatility ahead.

The S&P 500 recently entered correction territory on AI-related worries. President Trump blamed the market's roughly $6 trillion slide on Democratic midterm wins, writing on Truth Social that the market was down more than $6 trillion since the November 3 election. Democrats and many analysts instead point to concerns about AI valuations and spending.

Federal Reserve officials have warned that the AI boom is adding to inflation risks ahead of an expected December rate hike, adding to uncertainty for investors heading into the holiday week.
